title: Additive bases and complete sequences
summary: $A$ is a basis of order $h$ if every large integer is a sum of $h$ elements of $A$; $A$ is complete if every large integer is a sum of distinct elements. Lagrange, Waring and Goldbach are statements of this kind.
why: It is the additive counterpart of factorisation: which sparse sets still generate everything.
references: Erdős & Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory

title: Egyptian fractions
summary: Writing rationals as sums of distinct $1/n$. Every rational has such representations; the questions are how short, how small the denominators, and which colourings or dense sets must contain a representation of $1$.
key_statements: \text{any } r\text{-colouring of } \mathbb N \text{ has a monochromatic } \textstyle\sum 1/n_i = 1 \ \text{(Croot 2003)}
why: Bloom's 2021 density theorem, built on Croot's method, is a model of how analytic tools enter elementary-looking questions.
references: Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory
Erdős & Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory

timeline.title: Monochromatic Egyptian fractions
timeline.text: Any finite colouring of the integers has a monochromatic set with $\sum 1/n = 1$.

title: Covering systems
summary: A finite set of congruences $a_i \bmod n_i$ covering every integer, such as $0\bmod2,\ 0\bmod3,\ 1\bmod4,\ 5\bmod6,\ 7\bmod12$. Hough (2015) proved the smallest modulus of a covering with distinct moduli is bounded.
why: Coverings produce Sierpiński numbers (odd $k$ with every $k2^n+1$ composite) and are a test case for the probabilistic method.
references: Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory
Erdős & Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory

timeline.title: Covering systems introduced
timeline.text: Used a covering of $\mathbb Z$ by congruences to show a positive proportion of odd numbers are not $2^k+p$.

timeline.title: Minimum modulus of covering systems is bounded
timeline.text: Settled Erdős's minimum modulus problem negatively: distinct-moduli coverings have least modulus at most $10^{16}$.

title: Primitive sets
summary: A set of integers $>1$ in which no element divides another. Erdős proved $\sum 1/(a\log a)$ is bounded over primitive sets and conjectured the primes maximise it; Lichtman proved this in 2022.
why: It shows how a combinatorial condition (no divisibility) interacts with the multiplicative structure measured by Mertens-type sums.
references: Erdős & Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory

timeline.title: Erdős primitive set conjecture
timeline.text: The primes maximise $\sum 1/(a\log a)$ over primitive sets.

title: Discrepancy
summary: How evenly can a $\pm1$ sequence be balanced on a family of sets? Erdős asked whether $\sup_{n,d}|\sum_{k\le n} f(kd)|$ is unbounded for every $f:\mathbb N\to\{\pm1\}$; Tao proved it in 2015.
why: Tao's proof combined the Polymath5 reduction to multiplicative functions, an entropy decrement argument and the Matomäki–Radziwiłł theorem on short averages.

timeline.title: The Erdős discrepancy problem
timeline.text: Proved $\sup|\sum_{k\le n} f(kd)| = \infty$ for every $\pm1$ sequence, building on Polymath5.

title: Counting and bijections
summary: Counting a set by splitting it into cases, by a bijection with a set that is easier to count, or by inclusion–exclusion. Binomial coefficients are the basic language.
why: Every probability, every expected value and most extremal bounds start as a count.
references: Andreescu & Feng, A Path to Combinatorics for Undergraduates

title: Pigeonhole and double counting
summary: If $n+1$ objects go into $n$ boxes, some box gets two. Double counting evaluates one quantity in two ways, such as the number of (vertex, edge) incidences, to get an identity or inequality.
key_statements: \text{some box holds at least } \lceil N/k \rceil \text{ objects}
why: Both are the first move in extremal problems: they turn a structure into a count that cannot be too large.
references: Andreescu & Feng, A Path to Combinatorics for Undergraduates
